title: How to Hire a School Superintendent
author: Robert Pondiscio
summary: Robert Pondiscio, watching his own upstate New York district begin a superintendent search, sets out what a school board should ask when hiring its most consequential employee. His premise is that districts that stay high-performing share coherence, focus and resistance to change for change's sake, so leadership churn is the main threat to durability. He advises hiring for the specific problems the district must solve in five years, probing execution rather than vision, and asking what candidates said no to as a check on initiative churn. He wants candidates tested on whether they can describe a strong lesson and on the superintendent's role in selecting and monitoring curriculum, treating the superintendent as the de facto chief academic officer. He also recommends probing temperament, board relations and the candidate's real reason for wanting this district, citing Dylan Wiliam on leaders stopping good things to make room for better ones.
points: Boards should hire against the three or four concrete problems the district must solve, not against a generic profile of visionary leadership.
Interview questions should force candidates to describe what they actually delivered and stopped doing, because the distance between announcing and implementing a reform is vast.
Initiative churn is a hidden cost, and a candidate's willingness to say no is a better predictor of stability than a shiny new program.
The superintendent must be the instructional leader who understands curriculum and teaching, since a candidate who treats curriculum as procurement is unlikely to move outcomes.
Temperament and board relationships decide whether a capable superintendent survives long enough for reforms to take root.
quotes: Hiring a superintendent is the single most important decision a school board makes. The chief executive officer of a school district, the supe is responsible for overseeing operations, managing personnel and budgets, implementing board policies, and ensuring the effective administration of schools. He or she shapes not just policy but the daily experience of students and teachers for years to come.
Education rewards charismatic figures who can talk compellingly about change. School districts need people who have actually delivered it.
The gap between announcing a reform and implementing it is vast, and the classroom is where ideas—good, bad, and mediocre—go to die.
One of the most common, yet least discussed, features of school systems is initiative churn. Programs appear, disappear, and reappear either rebranded or in slightly different forms.
Raising student achievement is not one priority among many. It is the work of a school system and defines a quality district.

Dylan Wiliam often observes that when teachers are asked to identify something that they will stop doing or do less of to create time and space to improve their teaching, they fail miserably, concluding that everything they do contributes to student learning. “The essence of effective leadership is stopping people from doing good things to give them time to do even better things,” he wrote.
The lesson of durable success is not that schools need better ideas. It’s that they need the discipline to stick with good ones long enough to matter.
